fetched_contents.text: Burosumab and Dental Abscesses in Children With X‐Linked Hypophosphatemia ABSTRACT X‐linked hypophosphatemia (XLH) is a rare genetic disorder that disrupts skeletal and dental mineralization. In addition to rickets in children, XLH patients also have frequent spontaneous dental abscesses that increase the risk of tooth loss and may lead to facial cellulitis. Hypomineralized and hypoplastic dentin is the main driver of these infections. Conventional treatment (CT) of XLH improves this tissue defect and reduces the occurrence of dental abscesses. Burosumab is a recent treatment for XLH that targets excess circulating fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), and its benefits on rickets have been demonstrated. It is not yet known whether burosumab improves dental manifestations of XLH. The main objective of our study was to compare the incidence of dental abscesses with XLH treated with either CT or burosumab. In this monocentric retrospective study, we measured and compared the incidence of dental abscess in children with XLH treated with either CT or burosumab, followed at our dental center for at least 1 year. The primary endpoint was the number of dental abscesses per month of dental follow‐up. A total of 71 children were included in the study, with a mean ± standard deviation (SD) age at the start of dental follow‐up of 7.86 ± 3.76. Thirty‐eight children were treated with CT (53.5%) and 33 with burosumab (46.5%). All children treated with burosumab had previously been treated with CT. The mean number of dental abscesses per month of dental follow‐up was significantly reduced in the burosumab group compared with the CT group (0.01 versus 0.04; p = 0.04). Burosumab treatment appears to be associated with a reduction in the number of dental abscesses in XLH children, compared with CT. © 2022 The Authors. In children, these infections lead to dental abscesses, which translate clinically into painful swelling of the gum. Pediatric Endocrinology Volume 15 - 2024 | https://doi.org/10.3389/fendo.2024.1414509 Meta-analysis and systematic review: burosumab as a promising treatment for children with X-linked hypophosphatemia * KW Kangning Wang † * RZ Runze Zhang † * ZC Ziyi Chen † * YB Yi Bai * * QH Qing He * * State Key Laboratory of Oral & Maxillofacial Reconstruction and Regeneration, Key Laboratory of Oral Biomedicine Ministry of Education, Hubei Key Laboratory of Stomatology, School & Hospital of Stomatology, Wuhan University, Wuhan, China Article metrics View details Abstract Objective: The aim of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of burosumab therapy in children with X-Linked Hypophosphatemia (XLH). Materials and methods: We systematically reviewed literature from PubMed, Web of Science, The Cochrane Library, and Embase up until January 2024, using EndNote Web for study organization. The Newcastle–Ottawa scale guided quality assessment, while Revman software was used for data analysis and visualization. Study selection, quality evaluation, and data aggregation were independently performed by three researchers. Results: The meta-analysis encompassed ten studies, including eight cohort studies that examined burosumab’s impact pre- and post-administration, and two randomized controlled trials comparing burosumab to standard therapy. The evidence from this review suggests burosumab’s superiority in managing XLH in pediatric populations, particularly in improving key biochemical markers including 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25-(OH)2D), phosphorus, and alkaline phosphatase (ALP), alongside improvements in the renal tubular maximum reabsorption rate of phosphate to glomerular filtration rate (TmP/GFR), and significant skeletal improvements as indicated by the rickets severity score (RSS) and the 6-minute walk test (6MWT). However, the long-term safety and effects, including height and quality of life (QOL) data, remains to be elucidated. Conclusions: Burosumab has shown significant therapeutic effectiveness in treating children with XLH, highlighting its potential as a key treatment option. 1 Introduction X-linked hypophosphatemia (XLH) is a rare genetic disorder primarily caused by loss-of-function variants of phosphate-regulating endopeptidase gene on the X chromosome (PHEX) located on the X chromosome. It is the most common form of hereditary rickets and osteomalacia (1, 2), while other genetic factors can also contribute to hypophosphatemic rickets, including mutations in FGF23, DMP1, ENPP1, and FAM20C (3). With a prevalence of approximately 1 in 20,000 newborns, XLH presents significant clinical challenges (4, 5). The disorder’s primary manifestations in infancy include rickets and growth retardation, which evolve into more pronounced lower limb deformities during childhood and adolescence (6). Additionally, studies indicate that XLH children also suffer from bone pain, gait impairment, reduced range of motion of ankle/knee joint, tooth abscesses, and/or skull stenosis (6–8). XLH is characterized by reduced renal phosphate reabsorption, which can be reflected by TmP/GFR value (9, 10), and impaired production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25-(OH)2D), complicating its management (11–13). The conventional therapy of XLH is treating the patients with oral phosphate and active vitamin D to compensate for renal phosphate wasting and counter 1,25-(OH)2D deficiency (14). With traditional treatment methods, the serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) level can be successfully regulated to remain within the upper limit of normal values within a year (14). Additionally, this treatment has shown efficacy in improving bone deformities in 30% to 60% of patients, enhancing their growth velocity, and optimizing dentin mineralization (14–16). While this approach can modestly improve bone deformities and growth rates in pediatric patients, its efficacy varies, and long-term use is associated with significant adverse events, including hyperparathyroidism, hypercalciuria, renal calcinosis, and kidney stones (14, 17). Despite treatment, hypophosphatemia often remains unresolved, and full restoration of muscle function is not achieved. Due to insufficient response to medication, some children require corrective surgery on their lower limbs (18). Furthermore, the frequent dosing required for conventional treatment poses a significant hurdle in ensuring patient compliance, as phosphate must be taken several times a day. fetched_contents.text: X‐Linked Hypophosphataemia and Burosumab: A Systemic Disease With a New Treatment - Sandy - 2025 - Journal of Paediatrics and Child Health ABSTRACT X linked hypophosphataemia (XLH) is a systemic, chronic condition that significantly impairs quality of life. In XLH, a phosphate regulating endopeptidase homologue X-linked (PHEX) gene mutation leads to excess fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), causing hypophosphataemia and subsequent rickets, lower limb deformity, pain and other sequelae, however there are likely other non-FGF23 mediated mechanisms contributing to disease. Burosumab is an FGF23 inhibiting monoclonal antibody that has been shown to be significantly more effective in treating X linked hypophosphataemia than previously available treatment (“conventional therapy” with oral phosphate and active vitamin D). Clinical trials and real-world studies have shown that burosumab can improve lower limb deformity, growth, pain, exercise capacity, biochemistry, rickets, and quality of life. However, the full effect of burosumab on the lives of individuals with X linked hypophosphataemia is yet to be determined. How burosumab may impact some of the lesser understood clinical features, including dental abscesses, craniosynostosis, enthesopathy, and osteoarthritis, is unclear. Whether burosumab mitigates the risk of complications associated with conventional therapy (nephrocalcinosis and hyperparathyroidism) has also not been established. There are conflicting recommendations on who should receive burosumab, when they should start it, and for how long they should continue taking it. This review summarises what is known, and more importantly what is unknown, about burosumab use in X linked hypophosphataemia. We highlight important areas for future research to better understand the impact of burosumab in XLH, improve management of XLH, assess cost benefit of, and advocate for fair and equitable access to burosumab. 1 Introduction X-linked hypophosphataemia (XLH) is an X-linked dominantly inherited form of hypophosphataemic rickets, but it is more than a bone disorder of childhood. It is a systemic condition that affects an individual throughout their lifespan and has a significant impact on quality of life [1-3]. The recent introduction of burosumab, a monoclonal antibody against fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), has been a critical advance for the XLH community. Burosumab can transform the lives of those affected by XLH, with clinical trials and subsequent studies showing it is well tolerated and more effective than previous therapeutic options. The introduction of burosumab has also given health professionals managing this disorder an opportunity to review, reflect upon, and improve the clinical management of this disorder [4-6]. However, the full effect of burosumab on the lives of individuals with XLH is yet to be completely elucidated. This review summarises the current knowledge of burosumab in XLH and identifies areas to guide future research in the management of XLH. We will focus on the clinical features that are associated with a significant burden of disease for individuals with XLH, but for which the impact of long term burosumab is not known. 2 X-Linked Hypophosphataemia: A Systemic, Lifelong, Incompletely Understood Condition X-linked hypophosphataemia (XLH) is an X-linked dominantly inherited condition caused by a mutation in the phosphate regulating endopeptidase homologue X-linked (PHEX) gene. XLH imparts a range of clinical symptoms and signs and there is wide phenotypic variation even within affected families. The most common clinical features are musculoskeletal, such as lower leg bowing, musculoskeletal pain, short stature, and impaired motor function. Other manifestations include dental abscesses, craniosynostosis, and Chiari I malformation. Affected adults have a risk of osteoarthritis, pseudofractures, periodontitis, enthesopathies, hearing impairment, obesity, hypertension, and spinal stenosis [1-3, 7-14]. Psychosocial and mental health impacts of the disease, including a negative effect on quality of life, are being increasingly recognised, but are still largely underreported and often overlooked [4, 11, 15, 16]. Prevalence estimates of XLH in the world literature range from 0.5 to 4.8 per 100 000 population [1, 17-21]. A recent report by the Australian Paediatric Surveillance Unit (ASPU) estimated a conservative minimum prevalence of 1.33 per 100 000, with the actual prevalence likely to be closer to 1.91 when taking into account predicted rates of ascertainment and undiagnosed cases [1]. In XLH, mutations in the PHEX gene lead to an increase in FGF23 expression via mechanisms that are not yet fully described. Elevated FGF23 induces chronic renal phosphate wasting through reducing the expression of type II sodium-phosphate co-transporters. FGF23 also inhibits the conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to active form 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, therefore reducing gastrointestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate [7]. In XLH, chronic hypophosphataemia secondary to FGF23 leads to impaired bone mineralisation, causing rickets in children and osteomalacia in both children and adults. In teeth, hypophosphataemia leads to odontomalacia, a defect in mineralisation of dentin and cementum. There are also FGF23-independent effects of reduced PHEX function which lead to impaired bone matrix mineralisation and may contribute to other clinical features seen in XLH [2, 7]. While XLH is a rare disorder with a wide variability in severity of disease, it can profoundly impact an affected individual's quality of life. Until recent introduction of burosumab as a therapeutic option, treatment for XLH consisted of multiple daily doses of phosphate and activated vitamin D such as calcitriol or alfacalcidol (referred to as “conventional management”). Mini-report on the evidence base for burosumab and conventional therapies in children

The evidence base is concentrated on children with X-linked hypophosphatemia (XLH), a rare genetic disorder that disrupts skeletal and dental mineralization. XLH is important because it is associated with frequent spontaneous dental abscesses, which increase the risk of tooth loss, facial cellulitis, and poor quality of life, especially in children [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The studies are therefore focused on a specific rare condition rather than a general pediatric population. This makes the findings highly relevant for XLH but not directly generalizable to other conditions where dental abscesses may arise from different pathophysiology [N1-F1][N5-F3].

Study design, population, and follow-up duration
The evidence comes from a mix of observational and clinical study designs. The most directly relevant study is a monocentric retrospective study of 71 children with XLH, with a mean age of 7.86 years, followed for at least 1 year [N1-F1]. Another prospective case-control study explored burosumab’s effect on dental health in children with XLH [N2-R2]. The Canada Drug Agency review notes that systematic reviews and longer-term evidence are part of the broader evidence base, and it includes studies with different follow-up periods and design types, such as clinical trials and real-world studies [N5-F4]. The follow-up duration is therefore not uniform: some studies are short-term, while others extend beyond a year [N1-F1][N5-F4].

Main outcome measures used for abscesses and related oral health outcomes
The primary outcome in the key XLH study was the number of dental abscesses per month of dental follow-up [N1-F1]. It also reported prevalence and incidence of dental abscesses, as well as cellulitis of odontogenic origin [N1-F1]. Related oral health outcomes include developmental defects of enamel and dentin, dental caries, taurodontism, large pulp chambers, and periodontitis [N2-R5]. The literature also mentions broader dental health improvements such as improved dentin mineralization and reduced premature tooth loss with conventional therapy [N3-R3][N5-F3]. In the systematic review, outcomes include biochemical markers, rickets severity, growth, pain, exercise capacity, and quality of life, with some mention of complications such as nephrocalcinosis and hyperparathyroidism [N5-F2]. Overall, the evidence uses both abscess-specific measures and broader dental/clinical endpoints [N1-F1][N2-R5][N5-F2].

Bottom line
The evidence base is strongest for XLH children and focuses on dental abscesses as a clinically important outcome. The main study designs are observational and retrospective in some cases, while broader comparative evidence includes systematic reviews and longer-term follow-up. The outcome measures are primarily dental abscesses and related oral health features, but also broader skeletal and quality-of-life endpoints [N1-F1][N2-R2][N5-F2].

Compare prevalence and incidence effects across follow-up periods

Across the evidence provided, prevalence and incidence change over time, but the direction and magnitude differ by study design and follow-up duration. The most directly relevant study is a retrospective, monocentric study in children with XLH, where the primary endpoint was the number of dental abscesses per month of dental follow-up [N1-F1]. In that study, burosumab was associated with a significantly lower monthly rate of abscesses than conventional therapy (0.01 vs. 0.04 per month; p = 0.04) [N1-F1]. The same study also reported that dental abscesses were very high in the study population, with 40.8% of children presenting with at least one abscess during the dental follow-up [N1-R1]. This suggests that, in this cohort, abscesses were common at baseline and were being measured as a recurrent rather than a one-time event [N1-R1][N1-F1].

The follow-up period matters because longer observation can capture sustained effects versus transient ones. The study required at least 1 year of dental follow-up, and the analysis was based on that follow-up period [N1-F1]. A later report also states that, after transitioning to burosumab therapy, prevalence of dental abscesses decreased to 10.00% after one year and remained steady after three years [N2-R5]. This supports the idea that the effect may persist beyond a single year, but it also depends on how the outcome is measured. If prevalence is defined as the proportion of children with at least one episode during a defined period, then a lower prevalence may reflect reduced occurrence rather than elimination [N2-R5]. # How do burosumab and conventional therapies compare in their effects on the prevalence and incidence of dental abscesses in children over different follow-up periods?

## Overall conclusion
The evidence provided suggests that, in children with **X-linked hypophosphatemia (XLH)**, **burosumab appears to reduce the prevalence and incidence of dental abscesses relative to conventional therapy**, but the evidence is limited, heterogeneous, and mostly centered on a rare condition. The observed benefit is strongest in short-term follow-up, and longer follow-up indicates persistence of the effect, though long-term safety and some outcomes remain incompletely understood [N1-F1][N2-R5][N5-F2]. However, the evidence also shows heterogeneity across studies, so the comparison should be interpreted cautiously.

## 1) Which condition is the evidence focused on, and why dental abscesses matter
The evidence base is concentrated on **children with XLH**, a rare genetic disorder that disrupts skeletal and dental mineralization [N1-F1][N5-F3]. In XLH, dental abscesses are clinically important because they are **frequent, recurrent, and associated with tooth loss, facial cellulitis, and poor quality of life** [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The condition also involves **hypomineralized and hypoplastic dentin, enlarged pulp chambers, and microcracks**, which make teeth more susceptible to infection [N1-F1]. This means that dental abscesses are not a random pediatric problem; they are a specific complication of XLH and a major reason why treatment matters.

## 2) What do the studies say about prevalence and incidence of dental abscesses?
The most direct evidence comes from a **monocentric retrospective study** of 71 children with XLH, where the primary outcome was the number of dental abscesses per month of dental follow-up [N1-F1]. In that study, **burosumab was associated with a significantly lower monthly rate of abscesses than conventional therapy**: **0.01 versus 0.04 per month; p = 0.04** [N1-F1]. The same study also reported that **40.8% of children presented with at least one dental abscess during the dental follow-up** [N1-R1], indicating that abscesses were common at baseline.

A later report says that, after transitioning to burosumab therapy, **prevalence of dental abscesses decreased to 10.00% after one year and remained steady after three years** [N2-R5]. This supports the idea that burosumab can reduce abscess burden, and that the effect may persist over time. The same source also notes that **incidence of dental abscesses decreased in XLH children treated with burosumab for an average of 3.2 years** [N2-R3], reinforcing the sustained effect narrative.

The evidence is not confined to abscesses alone. Related oral health outcomes include **developmental defects of enamel and dentin, dental caries, taurodontism, and large pulp chambers** [N2-R5]. This means the treatment effects are broader than abscesses, but abscesses remain a central outcome because they are particularly painful and clinically important [N1-F1][N2-R5].

## 3) How do prevalence and incidence change over time in each treatment group?
Across the evidence, prevalence and incidence change over time, but the direction and magnitude differ by study design and follow-up duration.

- In the XLH study, **abscesses were very high in the study population** at baseline, with **40.8% of children presenting with at least one abscess during follow-up** [N1-R1]. This suggests that abscesses were a recurrent problem rather than a one-time event [N1-R1][N1-F1].
- Burosumab was associated with a **lower monthly rate of abscesses** than conventional therapy [N1-F1].
- After one year, **prevalence of dental abscesses decreased to 10.00%** and remained steady after three years [N2-R5].
- After 3.2 years of burosumab treatment, **incidence of dental abscesses decreased** [N2-R3].

In short, the evidence suggests that burosumab reduces the burden of dental abscesses early on, and the benefit may persist over at least one to three years [N1-F1][N2-R5][N2-R3]. However, the evidence is not long enough to prove that the effect lasts indefinitely or that it does not reverse after even longer follow-up.

## 4) Does longer follow-up reveal sustained or divergent effects?
Longer follow-up appears to reveal **sustained effects**, at least in the evidence provided.

- After one year, prevalence decreased to **10.00%**, and after three years it remained steady [N2-R5].
- After 3.2 years of burosumab treatment, incidence also decreased [N2-R3].
- This suggests persistence rather than a transient effect [N2-R5][N2-R3].

However, the evidence also notes that longer follow-up is needed to assess sustained effects fully, and that **long-term safety and some outcomes remain to be elucidated** [N5-F2]. This implies that the apparent persistence may be genuine, but it is not yet definitive.

## 5) What follow-up periods were reported and why they matter?
Follow-up periods vary across the evidence, and this is important for interpreting the results.

- The XLH study required **at least 1 year of dental follow-up** [N1-F1].
- One report uses **one-year and three-year follow-up** for prevalence and incidence [N2-R5].
- Another report cites **3.2 years of treatment duration** for incidence of dental abscesses [N2-R3].
- The systematic review and Canada Drug Agency review note that evidence includes **pre- and post-administration studies** and that follow-up duration affects what can be concluded [N5-F2][N5-F4].

Why this matters: shorter follow-up may miss late-onset or reversing effects, while longer follow-up can show whether burosumab’s benefit persists or diverges from conventional therapy over time [N1-F1][N4-R5][N5-F2]. In this evidence set, follow-up of at least one year is common, but longer durations are needed for meaningful conclusions about sustained effects [N1-F1][N2-R5][N5-F2].

## 6) What does the comparative evidence say about conventional therapies?
Conventional therapy for XLH is described as **phosphorus and active vitamin D analogues**, and it has been shown to improve tissue defects and reduce the occurrence of dental abscesses [N3-R3][N5-F3]. In the XLH study, conventional therapy was the comparator arm, and the study explicitly states that burosumab is being compared with conventional therapy [N1-F1]. This makes conventional therapy the baseline against which burosumab is being evaluated.

The broader evidence also notes that conventional therapy has **modest efficacy, variable long-term response, and significant adverse events such as hyperparathyroidism, hypercalciuria, renal calcinosis, and kidney stones** [N5-F2]. This is important because it means that conventional therapy is not without risks, and burosumab may offer a better balance of efficacy and safety in some children [N5-F2].

## 7) What does the evidence say about children specifically?
The evidence is **strongest in children with XLH**, but it is not generalizable to all children or to all causes of dental abscesses. XLH is a rare genetic condition with a distinct pathophysiology, and dental abscesses in XLH are driven by **hypomineralized and hypoplastic dentin, enlarged pulp chambers, and microcracks** [N1-F1]. Therefore, the findings are highly specific to XLH and cannot be extrapolated broadly to other pediatric populations or other types of dental abscesses [N1-F1].

## 8) What are the methodological limitations and why they matter?
The evidence has several limitations that affect confidence in the comparisons.

- **Small sample size**: the XLH study included only 71 children, which is relatively small for a pediatric comparative study and may limit statistical power and generalizability [N1-F1][N6-R1].
- **Retrospective design**: the main study was monocentric and retrospective, which introduces selection bias, recall bias, and missing data issues [N1-F1][N6-R1].
- **Heterogeneous designs**: the evidence includes observational, clinical, cohort, and review-based studies, so the quality is not uniform [N1-F1][N5-F2].
- **Conflicting outcomes**: the evidence mentions conflicting oral health outcomes for burosumab, with studies variably reporting reduced rates of dental abscesses, no improvement, or other outcomes [N2-R4].
- **Incomplete long-term evidence**: long-term safety and effects remain to be fully elucidated, including height and quality-of-life data [N5-F2].

These limitations mean that the comparisons should be interpreted cautiously. The evidence is promising, but it is not definitive, and the apparent benefit of burosumab may be overestimated if the studies are not comparable.

## 9) Is the evidence consistent or conflicting?
The evidence is **mixed and heterogeneous**, but the direct comparisons in the provided materials are mostly consistent with a benefit of burosumab.

- **Reduced abscesses**: the XLH study showed a significantly lower monthly rate of abscesses with burosumab than with conventional therapy [N1-F1].
- **Reduced prevalence and steady incidence**: after one year, prevalence decreased to 10.00% and remained steady after three years [N2-R5].
- **Decreased incidence over 3.2 years**: incidence also decreased in burosumab-treated children [N2-R3].

However, the evidence also notes that **conflicting oral health outcomes have been reported** for burosumab, with studies variably reporting reduced rates of dental abscesses, no improvement, or other outcomes [N2-R4]. This heterogeneity suggests that not all studies support a uniform conclusion, and that some findings may be context-dependent.

## 10) What explains the apparent inconsistency?
The apparent inconsistency is best explained by several factors:

- **Diverse study designs**: the evidence includes observational, retrospective, cohort, and review-based studies, which differ in quality and interpretation [N1-F1][N5-F2].
- **Different follow-up periods**: shorter versus longer follow-up may capture different phases of the treatment effect [N1-F1][N2-R5][N5-F2].
- **Different outcomes**: some studies focus on abscesses, while others measure broader dental health, skeletal outcomes, or quality of life [N1-F1][N2-R5][N5-F2].
- **Differences in patient characteristics**: the study noted a difference in age at treatment initiation between groups, which may affect outcomes [N6-R1].
- **True heterogeneity**: the disease itself varies, and treatment effects may differ by age, baseline severity, and other factors [N1-F1][N5-F2].

In other words, the evidence is not inconsistent in a simple “all studies agree” way; it is heterogeneous because the studies are different in population, design, follow-up, and outcome [N1-F1][N2-R5][N5-F2][N6-R1].

## 11) What long-term follow-up and sustained effects are reported?
Long-term follow-up is used to assess both efficacy and safety.

- After one year, **prevalence decreased to 10.00%** and remained steady after three years [N2-R5].
- After 3.2 years of burosumab treatment, **incidence of dental abscesses decreased** [N2-R3].
- The systematic review and Canada Drug Agency review note broader long-term outcomes such as improved 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, renal tubular phosphate reabsorption, rickets severity, growth, pain, exercise capacity, and quality of life [N5-F2][N5-F4].
- They also note that long-term safety and effects remain to be fully elucidated, especially height and quality-of-life data [N5-F2].

So, the evidence supports **persistence of some effects** over time, but not enough to conclude that all effects are irreversible or permanent [N2-R5][N5-F2].

## 12) What follow-up durations are needed for meaningful conclusions?
Meaningful conclusions require follow-up durations that can capture both short-term and long-term effects.

- **At least one year** is commonly used and is useful for initial assessment [N1-F1][N2-R5].
- Some studies extend to **three years** or longer [N2-R5].
- The systematic review and Canada Drug Agency review emphasize that longer follow-up is needed to assess sustained effects and safety, including long-term safety and quality-of-life data [N5-F2][N5-F4].
- The evidence also notes that **later treatment may have less effect on dental abscesses**, and that follow-up duration matters for determining whether a treatment effect is durable [N8-R4].

Therefore, **follow-up durations of at least one year are useful**, but **longer follow-up—possibly several years—is needed** to determine whether effects persist or change over time [N1-F1][N2-R5][N5-F2][N8-R4].

## 13) Bottom line: how do burosumab and conventional therapies compare?
In children with **XLH**, the evidence suggests that **burosumab is associated with lower prevalence and incidence of dental abscesses compared with conventional therapy**, at least in the short to medium term [N1-F1][N2-R5][N2-R3]. However:

- The evidence is **limited and heterogeneous**, with a mix of observational, clinical, and review-based studies [N1-F1][N5-F2].
- The benefit appears **sustained over at least one to three years**, but long-term safety and some outcomes remain to be fully understood [N2-R5][N5-F2].
- The findings are **specific to XLH** and cannot be generalized to all children or all causes of dental abscesses [N1-F1].
- There is some **conflicting evidence** and heterogeneity across studies, so the comparisons should be interpreted cautiously [N2-R4][N5-F2].

## Final summary
If you want a simple answer: **burosumab appears to reduce dental abscess prevalence and incidence in children with XLH compared with conventional therapy, and the benefit may persist over at least one to three years, but the evidence is limited, heterogeneous, and specific to XLH.** [N1-F1][N2-R5][N5-F2]

If you want a more cautious answer: **the evidence is promising, but not definitive; burosumab may reduce dental abscesses in XLH children, and longer follow-up supports persistence, but the evidence base is small, heterogeneous, and needs more long-term studies to be fully confident.** [N1-F1][N2-R5][N5-F2]

Mini-report on the evidence base for burosumab and conventional therapies in children

The evidence base is concentrated on children with X-linked hypophosphatemia (XLH), a rare genetic disorder that disrupts skeletal and dental mineralization. XLH is important because it is associated with frequent spontaneous dental abscesses, which increase the risk of tooth loss, facial cellulitis, and poor quality of life, especially in children [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The studies are therefore focused on a specific rare condition rather than a general pediatric population. This makes the findings highly relevant for XLH but not directly generalizable to other conditions where dental abscesses may arise from different pathophysiology [N1-F1][N5-F3].

Study design, population, and follow-up duration
The evidence comes from a mix of observational and clinical study designs. The most directly relevant study is a monocentric retrospective study of 71 children with XLH, with a mean age of 7.86 years, followed for at least 1 year [N1-F1]. Another prospective case-control study explored burosumab’s effect on dental health in children with XLH [N2-R2]. The Canada Drug Agency review notes that systematic reviews and longer-term evidence are part of the broader evidence base, and it includes studies with different follow-up periods and design types, such as clinical trials and real-world studies [N5-F4]. The follow-up duration is therefore not uniform: some studies are short-term, while others extend beyond a year [N1-F1][N5-F4].

Main outcome measures used for abscesses and related oral health outcomes
The primary outcome in the key XLH study was the number of dental abscesses per month of dental follow-up [N1-F1]. It also reported prevalence and incidence of dental abscesses, as well as cellulitis of odontogenic origin [N1-F1]. Related oral health outcomes include developmental defects of enamel and dentin, dental caries, taurodontism, large pulp chambers, and periodontitis [N2-R5]. The literature also mentions broader dental health improvements such as improved dentin mineralization and reduced premature tooth loss with conventional therapy [N3-R3][N5-F3]. In the systematic review, outcomes include biochemical markers, rickets severity, growth, pain, exercise capacity, and quality of life, with some mention of complications such as nephrocalcinosis and hyperparathyroidism [N5-F2]. Overall, the evidence uses both abscess-specific measures and broader dental/clinical endpoints [N1-F1][N2-R5][N5-F2].

Bottom line
The evidence base is strongest for XLH children and focuses on dental abscesses as a clinically important outcome. The main study designs are observational and retrospective in some cases, while broader comparative evidence includes systematic reviews and longer-term follow-up. The outcome measures are primarily dental abscesses and related oral health features, but also broader skeletal and quality-of-life endpoints [N1-F1][N2-R2][N5-F2].

Compare prevalence and incidence effects across follow-up periods

Across the evidence provided, prevalence and incidence change over time, but the direction and magnitude differ by study design and follow-up duration. The most directly relevant study is a retrospective, monocentric study in children with XLH, where the primary endpoint was the number of dental abscesses per month of dental follow-up [N1-F1]. In that study, burosumab was associated with a significantly lower monthly rate of abscesses than conventional therapy (0.01 vs. 0.04 per month; p = 0.04) [N1-F1]. The same study also reported that dental abscesses were very high in the study population, with 40.8% of children presenting with at least one abscess during the dental follow-up [N1-R1]. This suggests that, in this cohort, abscesses were common at baseline and were being measured as a recurrent rather than a one-time event [N1-R1][N1-F1].

The follow-up period matters because longer observation can capture sustained effects versus transient ones. The study required at least 1 year of dental follow-up, and the analysis was based on that follow-up period [N1-F1]. A later report also states that, after transitioning to burosumab therapy, prevalence of dental abscesses decreased to 10.00% after one year and remained steady after three years [N2-R5]. This supports the idea that the effect may persist beyond a single year, but it also depends on how the outcome is measured. If prevalence is defined as the proportion of children with at least one episode during a defined period, then a lower prevalence may reflect reduced occurrence rather than elimination [N2-R5]. The same report also notes that other studies have reported dental abscesses, developmental defects, dental caries, taurodontism, and large pulp chambers, but it does not quantify how these change over time [N2-R5].

Longer follow-up may reveal sustained or divergent effects. The study cited in N2-R5 suggests that the effect remained steady after three years, implying persistence rather than regression [N2-R5]. However, the evidence does not provide a direct head-to-head comparison of burosumab versus conventional therapy across very long follow-up periods. The meta-analysis and systematic review note that burosumab has been studied pre- and post-administration, with some evidence from cohort studies and two randomized controlled trials comparing burosumab with standard therapy [N5-F2]. It also notes that long-term safety and effects remain to be fully elucidated, including height and quality of life data [N5-F2]. This indicates that follow-up periods longer than one year are needed to assess sustained effects, but the evidence base is still limited for very long-term comparisons [N5-F2].

Why follow-up periods matter
Follow-up periods matter because incidence density and prevalence depend on how long children are observed. The evidence provided emphasizes that follow-up duration affects whether a treatment effect is detected, whether it is sustained, and whether a one-time event is distinguished from recurrent events [N1-F1][N4-R5]. Short follow-up may miss late-onset or reversing effects, while longer follow-up can show whether burosumab’s benefit persists or diverges from conventional therapy over time. The cited systematic review also highlights that follow-up duration is a factor in determining what outcomes can be assessed and how robust the conclusions are [N5-F2]. In this evidence set, follow-up of at least one year is common, but longer durations are needed for meaningful conclusions about sustained effects [N1-F1][N2-R5][N5-F2].

Study quality issues such as sample size, bias, and missing data
The evidence base includes both observational and clinical studies, which implies different quality profiles. The most directly relevant study is a monocentric retrospective study of 71 children with XLH [N1-F1]. Retrospective designs are vulnerable to selection bias, recall bias, and missing data, and the study notes that a limitation was the difference in age at treatment initiation between the CT and burosumab groups [N6-R1]. Another study mentioned that a conventional therapy group improved tissue defects and reduced occurrence of dental abscesses, but the evidence item does not provide enough detail to assess sample size or missing data explicitly [N3-R3]. The systematic review and Canada Drug Agency review indicate that evidence comes from multiple study types, including cohort studies and randomized controlled trials, but the review also notes that long-term safety and some outcomes remain to be elucidated [N5-F2][N5-F4]. Overall, the evidence is heterogeneous in design quality, with the strongest direct evidence being a single retrospective study and some weaker observational or review-based comparative evidence [N1-F1][N5-F2].

How well the evidence applies to children and to dental abscess outcomes
The evidence is highly relevant to children, because all the studies are specifically about children with XLH and because the outcomes are pediatric dental abscesses, developmental defects, caries, pulp chambers, and related oral health features [N1-F1][N2-R5]. However, the evidence is not generalizable to all children or to all causes of dental abscesses. The studies are focused on XLH, a rare genetic condition with a distinct pathophysiology of hypomineralized and hypoplastic dentin, enlarged pulp chambers, and microcracks that favor infection [N1-F1]. Dental abscesses in XLH are therefore not representative of abscesses from other pediatric conditions such as trauma, caries, or infection in normally mineralized teeth [N1-F1]. This means the findings are highly specific to XLH and cannot be extrapolated broadly.

Limitations that affect confidence in the comparisons
The main limitations affecting confidence are limited sample size, possible selection bias, and incomplete follow-up. The monocentric study had 71 children, which is relatively small for a pediatric comparative study and may limit statistical power and generalizability [N1-F1][N6-R1]. Retrospective design also introduces recall and missing data issues, as noted by the authors [N6-R1]. The evidence set also includes conflicting oral health outcomes reported for burosumab, with studies variably reporting reduced rates of dental abscesses, no improvement, or other outcomes [N2-R4]. This heterogeneity weakens the confidence in a single conclusion and suggests that the comparisons are not fully consistent across studies [N2-R4]. The Canada Drug Agency review notes that some gaps in the evidence remain, including longer-term safety and quality-of-life data, and that follow-up duration affects what can be concluded [N5-F2][N5-F4]. ## Overall conclusion
The evidence provided suggests that, in children with **X-linked hypophosphatemia (XLH)**, **burosumab appears to reduce the prevalence and incidence of dental abscesses relative to conventional therapy**, but the evidence is limited, heterogeneous, and mostly centered on a rare condition. The observed benefit is strongest in short-term follow-up, and longer follow-up indicates persistence of the effect, though long-term safety and some outcomes remain incompletely understood [N1-F1][N2-R5][N5-F2]. However, the evidence also shows heterogeneity across studies, so the comparison should be interpreted cautiously.

The evidence base is concentrated on **children with XLH**, a rare genetic disorder that disrupts skeletal and dental mineralization [N1-F1][N5-F3]. In XLH, dental abscesses are clinically important because they are **frequent, recurrent, and associated with tooth loss, facial cellulitis, and poor quality of life** [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The condition also involves **hypomineralized and hypoplastic dentin, enlarged pulp chambers, and microcracks**, which make teeth more susceptible to infection [N1-F1]. This means that dental abscesses are not a random pediatric problem; they are a specific complication of XLH and a major reason why treatment matters.

## 2) What do the studies say about prevalence and incidence of dental abscesses?
The most direct evidence comes from a **monocentric retrospective study** of 71 children with XLH, where the primary outcome was the number of dental abscesses per month of dental follow-up [N1-F1]. In that study, **burosumab was associated with a significantly lower monthly rate of abscesses than conventional therapy**: **0.01 versus 0.04 per month; p = 0.04** [N1-F1]. The same study also reported that **40.8% of children presented with at least one dental abscess during the dental follow-up** [N1-R1], indicating that abscesses were common at baseline.

A later report says that, after transitioning to burosumab therapy, **prevalence of dental abscesses decreased to 10.00% after one year and remained steady after three years** [N2-R5]. This supports the idea that burosumab can reduce abscess burden, and that the effect may persist over time. This means the treatment effects are broader than abscesses, but abscesses remain a central outcome because they are particularly painful and clinically important [N1-F1][N2-R5].

## 3) How do prevalence and incidence change over time in each treatment group?
Across the evidence, prevalence and incidence change over time, but the direction and magnitude differ by study design and follow-up duration.

- In the XLH study, **abscesses were very high in the study population** at baseline, with **40.8% of children presenting with at least one abscess during follow-up** [N1-R1]. This suggests that abscesses were a recurrent problem rather than a one-time event [N1-R1][N1-F1].

- After one year, **prevalence of dental abscesses decreased to 10.00%** and remained steady after three years [N2-R5].
- After 3.2 years of burosumab treatment, **incidence of dental abscesses decreased** [N2-R3].

However, the evidence is not long enough to prove that the effect lasts indefinitely or that it does not reverse after even longer follow-up.

The evidence base is strongest for XLH children and focuses on dental abscesses as a clinically important outcome. ## Overall conclusion
The evidence provided suggests that, in children with **X-linked hypophosphatemia (XLH)**, **burosumab appears to reduce the prevalence and incidence of dental abscesses relative to conventional therapy**, but the evidence is limited, heterogeneous, and mostly centered on a rare condition. The observed benefit is strongest in short-term follow-up, and longer follow-up indicates persistence of the effect, though long-term safety and some outcomes remain incompletely understood [N1-F1][N2-R5][N5-F2]. ## 1) Which condition is the evidence focused on, and why dental abscesses matter
The evidence base is concentrated on **children with XLH**, a rare genetic disorder that disrupts skeletal and dental mineralization [N1-F1][N5-F3]. In XLH, dental abscesses are clinically important because they are **frequent, recurrent, and associated with tooth loss, facial cellulitis, and poor quality of life** [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The condition also involves **hypomineralized and hypoplastic dentin, enlarged pulp chambers, and microcracks**, which make teeth more susceptible to infection [N1-F1]. This means that dental abscesses are not a random pediatric problem; they are a specific complication of XLH and a major reason why treatment matters.

## 2) What do the studies say about prevalence and incidence of dental abscesses?
The most direct evidence comes from a **monocentric retrospective study** of 71 children with XLH, where the primary outcome was the number of dental abscesses per month of dental follow-up [N1-F1]. A later report says that, after transitioning to burosumab therapy, **prevalence of dental abscesses decreased to 10.00% after one year and remained steady after three years** [N2-R5]. This supports the idea that burosumab can reduce abscess burden, and that the effect may persist over time. The same source also notes that **incidence of dental abscesses decreased in XLH children treated with burosumab for an average of 3.2 years** [N2-R3], reinforcing the sustained effect narrative.

This means the treatment effects are broader than abscesses, but abscesses remain a central outcome because they are particularly painful and clinically important [N1-F1][N2-R5].

## 3) How do prevalence and incidence change over time in each treatment group?
Across the evidence, prevalence and incidence change over time, but the direction and magnitude differ by study design and follow-up duration.

- In the XLH study, **abscesses were very high in the study population** at baseline, with **40.8% of children presenting with at least one abscess during follow-up** [N1-R1]. This suggests that abscesses were a recurrent problem rather than a one-time event [N1-R1][N1-F1].

- After 3.2 years of burosumab treatment, **incidence of dental abscesses decreased** [N2-R3].

However, the evidence is not long enough to prove that the effect lasts indefinitely or that it does not reverse after even longer follow-up.

## 4) Does longer follow-up reveal sustained or divergent effects?
